_note: “Did you know?” box on the printable sheet of a word set (src/pages/vocabulary/print/[set].astro): two or three short facts about Spanish and life in Spain, tied to the words of the unit, in the English of the level. Machine draft 2026-11-06, not yet reviewed by a teacher.
a1-01: Most people in Spain have two ‘apellidos’: usually the father's first, then the mother's.
Spanish uses ‘tener’ for age: ‘Tengo treinta años’ means ‘I have thirty years’.
‘Cumpleaños’ is the same in the singular and the plural: ‘un cumpleaños’, ‘dos cumpleaños’.
a1-02: ‘Los hermanos’ can mean brothers, or brothers and sisters together.
‘Mujer’ means ‘woman’ and also ‘wife’: ‘mi mujer’ is ‘my wife’.
Among friends in Spain, ‘tío’ and ‘tía’ also mean ‘guy’ and ‘girl’, not only ‘uncle’ and ‘aunt’.
a1-03: ‘Estar aburrido’ means to be bored. ‘Ser aburrido’ means to be boring.
‘El problema’ ends in -a but is masculine: ‘un problema’, not ‘una problema’.
‘Contento’ and ‘feliz’ both mean happy. ‘Feliz’ is the same for men and women.
a1-04: In an address, ‘3.º B’ means third floor, door B. The ground floor is ‘bajo’.
In Spain people live in a ‘piso’. Many Latin American countries say ‘departamento’ or ‘apartamento’.
‘El baño’ has a bath or a shower. ‘El aseo’ is a small room with a toilet and a sink.
a1-05: Spain says ‘la nevera’ for the fridge. Mexico often says ‘el refrigerador’, Argentina ‘la heladera’.
‘Un mueble’ is one piece of furniture. ‘Los muebles’ means furniture in general.
a1-06: ‘Agua’ is feminine but takes ‘el’: ‘el agua fría’, but ‘las aguas’.
Spanish uses ‘tener’ for hunger: ‘Tengo hambre’ means ‘I am hungry’.
a1-07: In Spain prices are written with a comma, and the euro sign comes after: 2,50 €.
‘Las rebajas’ are the sales. The big ones usually come in January and in summer.
a1-08: Spain says ‘jersey’ for a sweater. In Latin America many people say ‘suéter’.
For clothes you ask for your ‘talla’. For shoes in Spain you ask for your ‘número’.
Colours agree with the noun: ‘una camisa roja’, ‘unos zapatos negros’.
a1-09: ‘La mano’ ends in -o but is feminine: ‘la mano’, ‘las manos’.
With ‘doler’ the body part is the subject: ‘Me duele la cabeza’, ‘Me duelen los pies’.
Spanish uses ‘estar’ for health: ‘Estoy enfermo’, not ‘Soy enfermo’.
a1-10: 112 is the emergency number in Spain, and in the whole European Union.
Many places, also a ‘centro de salud’, ask for a ‘cita previa’: an appointment before you come.
Your ‘tarjeta sanitaria’ is usually issued by the health service of your region.
a1-11: In Spain ‘la comida’ is the main midday meal, often around two o'clock.
Restaurants in Spain often start serving ‘la cena’ at about nine in the evening.
a1-12: Spain says ‘ordenador’. Latin America mostly says ‘computadora’ or ‘computador’.
‘La nómina’ is your monthly payslip. Landlords and banks often ask to see it.
‘La policía’ is the police force. One officer is ‘el policía’ or ‘la policía’.
a1-13: ‘Examen’ has no accent, but the plural has one: ‘exámenes’.
‘Los deberes’ is homework. In Latin America people often say ‘la tarea’.
‘Curso’ means course and school year. In Spain the school year starts in September.
a1-14: ‘Quedar’ means to arrange to meet: ‘Quedamos a las ocho’.
Say ‘jugar al fútbol’ but ‘tocar la guitarra’: ‘jugar’ for games, ‘tocar’ for instruments.
‘La afición’ means hobby, and also the fans of a team.
a1-15: ‘Pueblo’ means a village or small town, and also ‘a people’.
A ‘bar’ in Spain serves coffee and breakfast, not only drinks with alcohol.
‘Aparcamiento’ is the car park in Spain. In Mexico people say ‘estacionamiento’.
a1-16: Spain says ‘coche’. Many Latin American countries say ‘carro’, and Argentina says ‘auto’.
In Spain ‘coger el autobús’ is normal. In parts of Latin America ‘coger’ is rude; people say ‘tomar’.
‘Billete’ is a ticket for a bus, train or plane. A ticket for a film is an ‘entrada’.
a1-17: Spain says ‘gafas de sol’. Many Latin Americans say ‘lentes de sol’.
‘Extranjero’ means foreigner and also abroad: ‘viajar al extranjero’.
a1-18: Train and plane times often use the 24-hour clock, but people say ‘las ocho y media’ for 20:30.
Days and months are written with a small letter: ‘el lunes’, ‘marzo’.
Dates go day, month, year: 06/11/2026 is the sixth of November.
a1-19: Spanish uses ‘hacer’ for weather: ‘Hace sol’, ‘Hace frío’, ‘Hace viento’.
Temperatures in Spain are in degrees Celsius: ‘veinticinco grados’.
‘Estación’ is a station, and also a season: ‘estación del año’.
a1-20: A living fish is ‘un pez’. A fish on your plate is ‘pescado’.
‘La mascota’ is feminine, also for a male pet. It means a pet.
a1-21: ‘Oír’ is to hear and ‘escuchar’ is to listen. ‘Mirar’ is to look and ‘ver’ is to see.
‘Contar’ means to count and to tell: ‘contar hasta diez’, ‘contar un cuento’.
‘Estar’ is for place and for states that change: ‘Estoy en casa’.
a1-22: ‘Saber’ is to know how: ‘Sé nadar’. ‘Poder’ is to be able to: ‘Puedo nadar hoy’.
‘Volver’ means to come back. ‘Devolver’ means to give something back.
‘Me gustaría’ is a polite way to say what you want.
a1-23: ‘Bueno’ and ‘malo’ lose the -o before a masculine noun: ‘un buen día’, ‘un mal día’.
‘Rico’ means rich, and in Spain also tasty: ‘Está muy rico’.
a1-24: ‘A’ + ‘el’ becomes ‘al’, and ‘de’ + ‘el’ becomes ‘del’. They are the only two.
‘Para’ is for a goal: ‘Es para ti’. ‘Por’ is for a reason: ‘Gracias por todo’.
a1-25: A Spanish question has two marks: ‘¿Cómo te llamas?’ The first one is upside down.
‘Por qué’ in two words asks why. ‘Porque’ in one word means because.
‘Sí’ with an accent is yes. ‘Si’ without an accent is if.
a1-26: A Spanish ‘código postal’ has five digits. The first two show the province.
The ‘DNI’ is the identity card of Spanish citizens. Foreign residents get a ‘NIE’, an identity number.
The ‘padrón’ is the list of residents of a town. You register at the ‘ayuntamiento’: ‘empadronarse’.
a2-01: For a home, the ‘fianza’ is usually one month's rent. Your contract says the rest.
In flat ads, ‘exterior’ means the windows face the street, and ‘interior’ means they face an inner courtyard.
a2-02: ‘Invitar’ means to invite and also to pay for someone: ‘Te invito’ means ‘It's on me’.
‘Portero’ is a doorman or concierge, and also a football goalkeeper.
a2-03: ‘La plancha’ is the iron. ‘A la plancha’ on a menu means cooked on a hot griddle.
Spain says ‘grifo’ for the tap. Many Latin American countries say ‘llave’, and Argentina ‘canilla’.
‘La colada’ is a load of washing. ‘Tender la ropa’ means to hang it up to dry.
a2-04: ‘Aceite’ comes from Arabic, a language that left many words in Spanish.
‘Tomate’ comes from ‘tomatl’, a word of the Nahuatl language of Mexico.
a2-05: A ‘menú del día’ is a fixed-price lunch with a first course, a second course and dessert, often on weekdays.
‘Una caña’ is a small glass of draught beer. The name of the size changes from region to region.
In some places, for example Granada, a ‘tapa’ often comes free with your drink.
a2-06: ‘Estar de baja’ means to be on sick leave.
‘Urgencias’ is the emergency department. For a small problem go first to your ‘centro de salud’.
a2-07: Some medicines, for example antibiotics, need a ‘receta’. Others are sold ‘sin receta’.
A ‘prospecto’ is the leaflet in the medicine box, not a prospectus.
‘Tirita’ is a plaster in Spain. In many Latin American countries people say ‘curita’.
a2-08: With body parts Spanish uses the article: ‘Me lavo las manos’, not ‘Me lavo mis manos’.
‘Champú’ is the Spanish spelling of the English word ‘shampoo’. The plural is ‘champús’.
a2-09: In job ads ‘bruto’ is the salary before tax and ‘neto’ is what you receive.
People without a job are ‘en paro’. They can register as job seekers with the public employment service.
‘Vida laboral’ is the record of your jobs. You can ask the Seguridad Social for the ‘informe de vida laboral’.
a2-10: ‘Jubilarse’ comes from a Latin verb meaning ‘to shout with joy’.
‘Ocuparse de’ means to take care of something: ‘Me ocupo del informe’.
a2-11: ‘Aprobar un examen’ means to pass an exam. ‘Suspender’ means to fail it.
‘Matrícula’ means enrolment, and also the number plate of a car.
A foreign degree may need ‘homologación’ before it counts in Spain. The process depends on the degree and the country.
a2-12: A Spanish ‘IBAN’ starts with ES and has 24 characters.
‘Moneda’ means coin and also currency. ‘Billete’ means banknote and also ticket.
a2-13: ‘TIE’ stands for ‘Tarjeta de Identidad de Extranjero’. The card shows a date, and ‘caducar’ means to expire.
A ‘gestoría’ is a private office that does official paperwork for a fee.
‘Trámite’ and ‘gestión’ are everyday words for an official procedure.
a2-14: ‘Seguro’ means insurance, safe and sure. The context tells you which.
Every car needs at least basic third-party insurance, the ‘seguro obligatorio’.
Forms often say ‘en mayúsculas’: write in capital letters.
a2-15: In Spain people often answer the phone with ‘Dígame’. In Mexico many say ‘Bueno’.
Spain says ‘móvil’ for mobile phone. Latin America says ‘celular’.
A phone number in Spain has nine digits. The country code, ‘prefijo’, is +34.
a2-16: Spain says ‘portátil’ for laptop and ‘ratón’ for mouse. Latin America often says ‘laptop’ and ‘mouse’.
The RAE writes ‘wifi’ in lowercase, as a masculine noun: ‘el wifi’.
‘Clic’ is the Spanish spelling of ‘click’. The plural is ‘clics’.
a2-17: Many shops and services must keep a ‘hoja de reclamaciones’ for customers. Each region sets its own rules.
‘¿Te queda bien?’ asks if clothes fit or suit you. ‘Quedar bien’ also means to make a good impression.
a2-18: An ‘abono’ is a pass for public transport. Its name and rules differ from city to city.
‘Cercanías’ is the commuter train service of Renfe in many Spanish cities.
‘Autocar’ is a coach for long trips. ‘Autobús’ is a city bus.
a2-19: In Spain people say ‘carné de conducir’. The RAE spells ‘carné’; ‘carnet’ is also accepted.
The ‘ITV’ is the regular technical check of a vehicle.
a2-20: On the Camino de Santiago, pilgrims sleep in ‘albergues’.
‘Media pensión’ means a room with breakfast and one main meal.
a2-21: On ‘Nochevieja’ many people eat twelve grapes at midnight, one for each chime of the clock.
In Spain many children get presents on 6 January, ‘el Día de Reyes’. The ‘Reyes Magos’ are the Three Kings.
‘¡Felicidades!’ is for birthdays. ‘¡Enhorabuena!’ is for success, such as a new job.
a2-22: The sport ‘pádel’ has an accent in Spanish.
‘Hacer footing’ means to go jogging. The word looks English, but English speakers do not say it.
a2-23: Foreign films in Spain are often dubbed. ‘VOSE’ means the original version with Spanish ‘subtítulos’.
‘Entrada’ is a ticket for a film or a concert. It also means entrance.
‘El final’ is the end of a story. ‘La final’ is the last match of a competition.
a2-24: ‘Ser listo’ means to be clever. ‘Estar listo’ means to be ready.
a2-25: ‘Vergüenza’ has two dots on the ‘ü’, so the ‘u’ is pronounced: ‘ver-GUEN-za’.
Men say ‘encantado’ and women say ‘encantada’ when they meet someone.
‘¡Qué pena!’ means ‘What a pity!’ In Mexico ‘pena’ can also mean embarrassment.
a2-26: In many towns, yellow containers are for packaging, blue for paper and green for glass.
A ‘punto limpio’ is a recycling centre for big or dangerous things, such as old furniture or batteries.
a2-27: ‘Ir’ is to go, ‘irse’ is to leave: ‘Me voy’ means ‘I'm leaving’.
‘Dormir’ is to sleep. ‘Dormirse’ is to fall asleep.
a2-28: ‘Quería un café’ uses the imperfect, but it is a polite way to ask for something now.
In a bar in Spain, ‘¿Me pones una caña?’ is a normal, friendly way to order.
b1-01: ‘Finiquito’ is the final payment when a job ends. It usually covers pay and holiday days you are still owed.
Many jobs follow a ‘convenio colectivo’, an agreement for a whole sector or company.
In most jobs the employer has to keep a record of working hours. That is why many people ‘fichan’.
b1-02: At the doctor's, a ‘volante’ is a referral note to a specialist, not only a steering wheel.
‘Chequeo’ comes from English ‘check-up’, and the RAE accepts it.
An ‘ambulatorio’ is an outpatient clinic. Today many people say ‘centro de salud’.
b1-03: Contracts say ‘arrendador’ and ‘arrendatario’. In daily speech people say ‘casero’ and ‘inquilino’.
‘VPO’ stands for ‘vivienda de protección oficial’: subsidised housing with its own rules.
‘Suministros’ are the utilities: electricity, water and gas.
b1-04: Documents from abroad often need an ‘apostilla’, and sometimes a ‘traducción jurada’ by a sworn translator.
A ‘tasa’ is a fee for an administrative service. An ‘impuesto’ is a tax.
b1-05: A ‘grado’ is the usual first university degree. It normally takes four years.
b1-06: ‘Medio ambiente’ is two words, but the adjective is one word: ‘medioambiental’.
‘Apagón’ is a blackout. The ending ‘-ón’ often makes a word bigger or more sudden.
b1-07: ‘Bizum’ lets you send money from your phone to a phone number. Many banks in Spain offer it.
‘Estar sin blanca’ means to have no money. A ‘blanca’ was an old coin of little value.
‘La declaración de la renta’ is the yearly income tax return. The campaign is in spring and early summer.
b1-08: A ‘peaje’ is a toll. Many ‘autopistas’ have one; most ‘autovías’ are free.
Traffic reports talk about ‘retenciones’. In conversation people say ‘atasco’.
The Spanish stop sign says STOP, as in most countries.
b1-09: Words ending in -ista have one form for men and women: ‘el periodista’, ‘la periodista’.
The RAE writes ‘pódcast’ with an accent.
‘Titular’ is a headline, and also the holder of a card or an account.
b1-10: ‘Tirar una indirecta’ means to give a hint without saying things directly.
‘Una charla’ is a chat, and also a short talk, such as ‘una charla sobre salud’.
b1-11: ‘ONG’ stands for ‘organización no gubernamental’. The plural is ‘las ONG’, without an -s.
Most towns have ‘servicios sociales’. You can ask at the ‘ayuntamiento’ where the nearest centre is.
Many cities have a ‘centro cívico’, a community centre with classes and activities.
b1-12: A ‘notario’ is a public official. A house purchase is signed in front of one.
In Spain trial by jury exists only for some serious crimes.
‘Juicio’ means trial, and also judgement: ‘tener buen juicio’.
b1-13: Spain says ‘ajustes’ for phone settings. Latin America often says ‘configuración’.
‘Copia de seguridad’ is a backup. Latin America often says ‘respaldo’.
‘Informática’ is the Spanish word for computing. It joins ‘información’ and ‘automática’.
b1-14: A ‘peña’ is a club of friends or fans, for example for football or for the town festival.
‘Socio’ means member and partner. Members pay a ‘cuota’.
A ‘polideportivo’ is a sports centre, often run by the town hall.
b1-15: ‘Facturar’ means to check in luggage, and also to send an invoice.
The RAE accepts ‘ferri’, an adapted spelling of ‘ferry’.
b1-16: ‘La caja’ means box and also the checkout. People say ‘pasar por caja’ to pay.
b1-17: ‘Arraigo’ means ‘roots’. In immigration it names permits based on ties to Spain; rules change, so check the official page.
Spain says ‘echar de menos’. Many Latin American countries say ‘extrañar’.
‘Emigrar’ is to leave a country. ‘Inmigrar’ is to arrive in one.
b1-18: Spain's head of government is called ‘Presidente del Gobierno’, not ‘primer ministro’.
Voters elect the ‘concejales’ of a town, and they choose the ‘alcalde’.
Spain's Constitution defines the state as a parliamentary monarchy.
b1-19: ‘Un turismo’ is also an official word for a passenger car, not only ‘tourism’.
Everyday Spanish says ‘el paro’ for ‘el desempleo’.
‘Mano de obra’ means labour or workforce. Literally it is ‘hand of work’.
b1-20: A ‘refrán’ is a proverb, for example ‘A quien madruga, Dios le ayuda’.
A ‘romería’ is a pilgrimage to a shrine mixed with a country festival. El Rocío in Andalusia is a famous one.
b1-21: ‘Sueño’ means both ‘sleep’ and ‘dream’: ‘Tengo sueño’ means ‘I'm sleepy’.
‘Preguntarse’ is to wonder: ‘Me pregunto si…’ means ‘I wonder if…’.
‘Aprender de memoria’ means to learn by heart.
b1-22: ‘Hincar los codos’ means to study hard. Literally, it is to dig in your elbows.
For a twisted ankle you say ‘Me he torcido el tobillo’.
b1-23: In Spain ‘canguro’ is a babysitter as well as a kangaroo.
Officially a nursery is an ‘escuela infantil’, but many people still say ‘guardería’.
‘Familia numerosa’ is an official status that can bring discounts. The rules say who qualifies.
b1-24: ‘IVA’ is value added tax. Shop prices in Spain already include it.
‘Vale’ means OK, and also a voucher you can spend in a shop.
‘Descambiar’ is an everyday word for exchanging something you bought.
b1-25: Many old Spanish towns have a ‘plaza mayor’ in the centre.
Pavement is ‘acera’ in Spain, ‘vereda’ in Argentina and ‘banqueta’ in Mexico.
An ‘urbanización’ is often a private housing estate with a shared garden or pool.
b1-26: ‘Sierra’ means mountain range and also saw: a range can look like the teeth of a saw.
‘Tierra’ means earth, land and soil. ‘La Tierra’ with a capital letter is the planet.
b1-27: ‘DANA’ stands for ‘depresión aislada en niveles altos’, a weather term now common in Spanish news.
‘Calima’ is dusty haze from the Sahara, often seen in the Canary Islands and the south.
The RAE writes ‘arcoíris’ as one word, with an accent. ‘Arco iris’ is also accepted.
b1-28: ‘Tilde’ means accent mark, and also the wave over the ‘ñ’.
In some regions another language is co-official with Spanish. That is a ‘lengua cooficial’.
Spanish spelling is close to pronunciation, but ‘h’ is silent and ‘b’ and ‘v’ sound the same.
b1-29: ‘Algodón’ comes from Arabic, and so does English ‘cotton’.
‘Corbata’ comes from French ‘cravate’, which comes from ‘Croat’.
b1-30: Centuries are written in Roman numerals: ‘el siglo XXI’.
Mainland Spain uses central European time. The Canary Islands are one hour behind.
‘Agenda’ is a diary or planner. The list for a meeting is ‘el orden del día’.
b1-31: ‘La física’ is the science of physics. ‘El físico’ is a physicist.
‘Datos’ comes from Latin, but Spanish has a singular: ‘un dato’, ‘los datos’.
b1-32: Many contracts include two ‘pagas extra’, often in summer and at Christmas. Some employers spread them over twelve months.
‘Prima’ means a bonus and also a female cousin.
b1-33: ‘Alta’ takes ‘el’ in ‘el alta médica’, the hospital discharge, just like ‘el agua’.
b1-34: Many Spanish windows have a ‘persiana’, a roller shutter, as well as curtains.
‘IBI’ is a yearly local tax paid by the owners of a property.
Sockets in Spain are 230 volts with two round pins.
b1-35: Many procedures can be done online on the ‘sede electrónica’ of an office.
‘Darse de alta’ means to register or sign up. The opposite is ‘darse de baja’.
‘Ingreso mínimo vital’ is a national income benefit created by the state in 2020.
b1-36: ‘ESO’ is compulsory secondary education, for ages 12 to 16.
A ‘colegio concertado’ is privately run but partly paid for by the state.
School marks go from 0 to 10, and 5 is a pass.
b1-37: ‘La cuesta de enero’ is the hard month of January, when money is short after Christmas.
‘Pensión’ is a pension, and also a small cheap hotel.
‘Chollo’ is an everyday word for a bargain.
b1-38: Drivers in Spain must carry a reflective vest. Since 2026 a connected V-16 warning light replaces the old triangles.
‘Claxon’ started as a brand name, Klaxon.
A ‘carné por puntos’ is a licence with points that you lose after traffic offences.
b1-39: ‘Bulo’ is the everyday word in Spain for a hoax or fake story.
‘Fuente’ means source, fountain and serving dish.
‘De hecho’ means ‘in fact’. ‘Hecho’ is also the past participle of ‘hacer’.
b1-40: ‘Discutir’ means to argue, and also to discuss.
‘Compromiso’ means commitment, and also compromise, engagement or an appointment.
‘Perdona’ and ‘perdone’ are used to say sorry and to get someone's attention.
b1-41: Charity events are often called ‘solidario’: ‘una carrera solidaria’ is a race for a cause.
‘Refugio’ can be a shelter for animals, or a hut in the mountains.
b1-42: After a theft you file a ‘denuncia’. Insurers often ask for a copy.
Spain has the ‘Policía Nacional’, the ‘Guardia Civil’, local police and, in some regions, their own police.
b1-43: A ‘llave inglesa’ is an adjustable spanner. ‘Llave’ also means key.
Spain says ‘destornillador’ for a screwdriver. Mexico says ‘desarmador’.
b1-44: On the night of 23 June, ‘la noche de San Juan’, many towns light ‘hogueras’.
The RAE writes ‘récord’ and ‘pícnic’ with an accent.
Spain says ‘zapatillas de deporte’. In Mexico people say ‘tenis’.
b1-45: A ‘consigna’ is the left-luggage office at a station. The word also means a slogan or an order.
b1-46: ‘Sobremesa’ is the time spent talking at the table after a meal.
In the north, small bites on bread are often ‘pinchos’. In Basque the word is ‘pintxos’.
‘Casero’ means homemade for food, and also the landlord: ‘comida casera’, ‘el casero’.
b2-01: ‘Plantilla’ means the staff of a company, and also a template.
‘Alto cargo’ names senior people in companies and in public administration.
b2-02: Between EU countries there are no ‘aranceles’. Goods from outside the EU follow common EU rules.
English took ‘embargo’ from Spanish. In Spanish ‘sin embargo’ means ‘however’.
b2-03: Legal Spanish likes pairs of words: ‘daños y perjuicios’ means damages.
‘Responsabilidad civil’ is the duty to repair damage you cause to others. Many insurance policies cover it.
b2-04: Congress and Senate together are called ‘las Cortes Generales’.
A ‘moción de censura’ must propose a new candidate for head of government.
Laws and ‘reales decretos’ are published in the ‘BOE’, the official state gazette.
b2-05: ‘La España vaciada’ is a common phrase for inland rural areas that are losing people.
‘Ascensor social’ means ‘social lift’: the idea of moving up in society.
b2-06: Madrid hosted the UN climate summit, COP25, in December 2019.
‘Gravar’ with ‘v’ means to tax. ‘Grabar’ with ‘b’ means to record.
b2-07: ‘Cortafuegos’ is a firewall, and also a firebreak cut through a forest.
‘Cifrar’ is the traditional Spanish word for to encrypt. ‘Encriptar’ is also common.
b2-08: ‘Hipótesis’ is feminine and does not change in the plural: ‘las hipótesis’.
‘Aleatorio’ comes from Latin ‘alea’, which means a die.
b2-09: ‘Prensa amarilla’ is sensational news. ‘Prensa rosa’ is celebrity gossip.
A ‘tertulia’ on radio or TV is a panel of commentators who discuss the news.
‘Rueda de prensa’ means press conference. Latin America also says ‘conferencia de prensa’.
b2-10: A ‘catedrático’ is a senior university professor. The word comes from ‘cátedra’, the professor's chair.
Older degrees are called ‘licenciatura’. Today's first degree is a ‘grado’.
A ‘colegio mayor’ is a university hall of residence with its own traditions.
b2-11: ‘Cuarentena’ comes from ‘cuarenta’, forty, from the old forty-day isolation.
‘Confinamiento’ became an everyday word in Spain in March 2020.
‘Brote’ means outbreak and also the new shoot of a plant.
b2-12: ‘Me agobia’ is a very common way to say that something overwhelms you.
In Spain, 024 is a free helpline for people in suicidal crisis.
b2-13: ‘Asilo’ means asylum, and also an old-fashioned word for a care home.
After the Civil War ended in 1939, many Spaniards went into exile, many of them to Mexico.
A ‘forastero’ is someone from outside a place, such as a village.
b2-14: ‘Mecenas’ comes from Maecenas, a Roman who supported poets and artists.
‘Subasta’ comes from the Latin ‘sub hasta’, ‘under the spear’.
‘Lienzo’ means canvas, and also linen cloth.
b2-15: Spanish marks formality with ‘tú’ and ‘usted’. This is the first step in register.
Newspapers and agencies publish a ‘libro de estilo’ with their writing rules.
b2-16: An ‘okupa’ is a squatter in a property. The spelling with ‘k’ is part of the word.
‘Piso turístico’ is a flat rented to visitors. Cities regulate it in different ways.
b2-17: A ‘dehesa’ is open oak woodland used for grazing, typical of western Spain.
‘Vías pecuarias’ are public routes that were made for moving livestock.
Doñana, in Andalusia, is a national park with large wetlands, ‘humedales’.
b2-18: ‘Plusvalía’ means gain in value. In Spain it is also a local tax linked to selling urban property.
‘Letras del Tesoro’ are short-term bonds issued by the Spanish state.
b2-19: ‘AVE’ stands for ‘Alta Velocidad Española’, and ‘ave’ also means bird.
‘Bache’ is a pothole, and also a bad patch in life.
Many Spanish cities have a ‘zona de bajas emisiones’, where some cars may be restricted.
b2-20: With ‘silencio administrativo’, if an office does not answer in time, the law treats it as yes or no, depending on the procedure.
The ‘Defensor del Pueblo’ is the ombudsman, an independent office that receives complaints about public administrations.
To ‘subsanar’ is to correct a missing or wrong item in your application.
b2-21: ‘Jornada partida’ is a split shift with a long midday break. ‘Jornada continua’ has no long break.
‘Fijo discontinuo’ is a permanent contract for work that comes in seasons, such as tourism.
b2-22: ‘Fecha de caducidad’ means use by. ‘Consumo preferente’ means best before.
‘Anisakis’ is a parasite in some sea fish. Freezing the fish kills it.
Many employers ask for the ‘carné de manipulador de alimentos’ from staff who handle food.
b2-23: ‘La cantera’ is a quarry, and also the youth academy of a football club.
‘Descenso’ means going down, and also relegation to a lower league.
b2-24: ‘Padrastro’ means stepfather, and also a hangnail.
‘Dependencia’ names the Spanish system that supports people who need help with daily life.
b2-25: In many public primary schools the ‘comedor escolar’ serves lunch, and families can apply for help.
‘Clases particulares’ are private lessons given to one student or a small group.
b2-26: ‘Tira y afloja’ means pull and loosen: the give and take of a negotiation.
‘Punto muerto’ means deadlock, and also neutral gear in a car.
‘Ceder’ means to make concessions, and also to give way: ‘ceda el paso’.
b2-27: ‘Compañero’ means ‘someone who shares bread’, from Latin ‘cum’ and ‘panis’.
‘La moral’ means morale or ethics. ‘El moral’ is a mulberry tree.
b2-28: A ‘cuña publicitaria’ is a short radio advert. ‘Cuña’ means wedge.
‘Publicidad encubierta’, advertising disguised as something else, is not allowed by Spanish law.
b2-29: ‘Eólico’ comes from Aeolus, the Greek god of the winds.
‘Red Eléctrica’ is the company that operates Spain's high-voltage grid.
‘Aislar’ means both to insulate and to isolate.
b2-30: Many small companies are an ‘S. L.’, ‘sociedad limitada’. Large ones are often an ‘S. A.’, ‘sociedad anónima’.
The ‘cuota de autónomos’ is the monthly contribution of the self-employed. How it is calculated has changed, so check the official page.
‘Empresa emergente’ is the Spanish term for ‘start-up’.
b2-31: Spanish has several names for a living will: ‘testamento vital’, ‘instrucciones previas’, ‘voluntades anticipadas’.
‘Duelo’ means grief, and also a duel.
Spain regulated euthanasia by law in 2021, under strict conditions.
b2-32: ES-Alert is the system that sends emergency warnings to mobile phones in an affected area.
‘Marejada’ is a sea state on the scale used in Spanish weather bulletins, between ‘marejadilla’ and ‘fuerte marejada’.
b2-33: The ‘recurso de amparo’ is a complaint to the Constitutional Court about fundamental rights.
6 December is ‘el Día de la Constitución’, a public holiday.
The ‘Portal de la Transparencia’ is a public website with information about the government.
b2-34: Professionals use ‘derivar’ when they refer you to another service.
‘Desamparo’ literally means ‘lack of shelter’. In law it also names a child without protection.
b2-35: ‘Homologación’ and ‘convalidación’ both mean recognising studies, but they are used for different procedures.
‘Remesas’ is money that migrants send to relatives in their home country.
‘Tarjeta azul’ is the Spanish name for the EU Blue Card for highly qualified workers.
b2-36: ‘Cumbre’ means summit, and also the top of a mountain.
The Ibero-American Summits have brought together leaders from Spain, Portugal and Latin America since 1991.
‘Tirante’ means taut, and is used for tense relations.
b2-37: ‘Plagio’ comes from Latin ‘plagium’, the crime of stealing a person.
b2-38: ‘Acequia’, a water channel, comes from Arabic.
A ‘trasvase’ moves water between river basins. It is debated between regions.
‘Regadío’ is irrigated farming. ‘Secano’ is farming without irrigation.
b2-39: Since 2010 the RAE writes ‘guion’ without an accent.
The Goya Awards, Spain's national film awards, are named after the painter Goya.
‘Bolo’ is a musician's word for a gig.
b2-40: Since 2021 both parents in Spain have the same length of leave after a birth.
‘Consentir’ can mean to consent, or to spoil a child: ‘un niño consentido’.
b2-41: ‘Vaquero’ means cowboy, and ‘vaqueros’ are jeans. ‘Tela vaquera’ is denim.
‘Perder el hilo’ means to lose the thread of a conversation.
b2-42: The AEMET weather service uses warning colours: yellow, orange and red.
‘Gota fría’ is a popular name for the weather phenomenon that experts also call DANA.
AEMET gives names to major storms, in alphabetical order through the season.
b2-43: ‘Hito’ was originally a stone that marked a boundary. Now it means milestone.
b2-44: ‘Bochorno’ means both muggy heat and embarrassment.
‘Rumiar’ is what cows do. For people it means to brood over something.
‘Morriña’, from Galician, is a feeling like ‘añoranza’: homesickness for the place you left.
b2-45: The ‘OMIC’ is the municipal office where you can ask about consumer problems.
For most online purchases the ‘derecho de desistimiento’ lets you withdraw within 14 days.
‘Hurtar’ is stealing without force, as in shoplifting. ‘Robar’ is more general.
b2-46: ‘Palma’ is the palm of the hand and also a palm tree.
‘Puño’ means fist and also the cuff of a shirt.
‘Talón’ is the heel, and in Spain also a cheque.
b2-47: In official deadlines counted in days, ‘días hábiles’ do not include Saturdays, Sundays or public holidays.
‘Apurarse’ means to worry in Spain, but to hurry in much of Latin America.
b2-48: After a cancellation or a long delay, EU rules give you rights, and the airline must tell you about them.
‘Pinchazo’ is a puncture, and also an injection.
b2-49: A ‘nota simple’ is an extract of the property register. It shows the owner and any charges on the home, such as a mortgage.
‘Arras’ is a deposit when you agree to buy a home. The same word names the 13 coins in a Catholic wedding.
A ‘derrama’ is an extra charge for the owners in a block for building works.
b2-50: ‘BIC’ stands for ‘bien de interés cultural’, the highest protection status for heritage in Spain.
An ‘artesonado’ is a decorated wooden ceiling, common in mudéjar buildings.
‘Aguja’ means needle, and also the spire of a church.
b2-51: People drawn by lot staff the ‘mesa electoral’. It is a civic duty, with limited excuses.
Plenary sessions of town councils, ‘plenos municipales’, are usually open to the public.
b2-52: ‘A bombo y platillo’ means with a lot of noise and publicity.
Santiago Ramón y Cajal won the Nobel Prize in 1906 and is called the father of modern neuroscience.
b2-53: ‘ERTE’ is a temporary suspension or reduction of work. ‘ERE’ is a procedure for collective dismissals.
‘Falso autónomo’ is a worker treated as self-employed who in reality works like an employee.
‘Fiscal’ means fiscal, as in tax, and also public prosecutor.
b2-54: ‘Fianza’ is a rental deposit, and also bail: ‘libertad bajo fianza’.
Some people are entitled to a lawyer paid by the state, through the ‘turno de oficio’.
An ‘indulto’ is a pardon granted by the Government.
b2-55: ‘Trasto’ means junk, and ‘trastero’ is the storage room where you keep it.
When you buy a new appliance, the shop often takes the old one for recycling.
b2-56: ‘Oposiciones’ are public exams for permanent civil-service posts, for example for teachers.
‘Matrícula de honor’ is the top mark, above ‘sobresaliente’.
‘Empollar’ is everyday Spanish for to cram. An ‘empollón’ is a swot.
b2-57: ‘Algoritmo’ comes from the name of the Arabic mathematician al-Khwarizmi.
The RAE accepts ‘dron’, with the plural ‘drones’.
b2-58: The RAE accepts ‘trol’ for an internet troll. The plural is ‘troles’.
‘Etiquetar’ means to tag someone in a post.
b2-59: ‘Acta’ takes ‘el’: ‘el acta’ is the written record of a meeting.
‘Ruegos y preguntas’ is the usual last point of a meeting, like ‘any other business’.
b2-60: A ‘trabalenguas’ is a tongue twister, for example ‘Tres tristes tigres’.
English took words such as ‘mosquito’, ‘tornado’ and ‘canyon’ from Spanish.
